Checks all my boxes for what I enjoy: Open World, RPG, Medieval Universe, Good story to get you vested in the world, smooth and challenging combat, co-op play.... for me it has it all. To top it off, they have continued to support, expand, and improve the game since its release. Now, I have to admit, after almost 1000 hours of playing it, combat is feeling repetitive. With $50+ invested in it and it's DLC, that breaks out to about .06 cents an hour for entertainment. I can't say anything else has given me so much joy for so little amount of financial investment. I give it my highest recommendation and say purchase it immediately, and when on sale?!... well, you don't have to be a mercenary to see that it's become a no-brainer!

candidates.text: It's like battle brothers but with nice 3D graphics and no RNG. Combat feels balanced and animations smooth. The turn based mechanics feel good and having 100% hit rate makes it feel much more tactical like a game of chess. I like that the roster size is limited only by what you can support from feeding/paying, like a mercenary band. candidates.text: Before buying this game, spend 3 or 4 hours, or more, trying to figure out all the UI elements, what each character is, etc. The game so completely lacks a tutorial or any explanation about how to do things that it'll take you 2 hours to figure out what it's all about.After that, if you're like me, you'll realise you don't like the minigames such as clicking at the right time when the game stutters and makes you auto-lose, and that the combat requires placement and guesswork about whether your AoE will or will not reach the target.I don't like the fact you only have one attack type per character. You can use valor (shared resource) to use other attacks, but I feel limited in what I can do in combat.Try to get a feel for the combat, fighting enemies that are not complete pushovers or outnumbered.If you like the combat, go for it.Personnally, it's not for me and I wish the game had had semi-decent ergonomy so I could have asked for a refund by the time my opinion on the game was set.

candidates.title: Wartales review
candidates.text: Because of quite positive press around Wartales I probably had too high hopes for it: an emergent story-driven game with moderately complex survival and interesting tactics elements in a somewhat unique medieval world. After playing for two hours of it, I can say Wartales is all of these things, but simply not to the level that is needed. The story does not really emerge due to the relatively flat characters and their unimpactful traits and interpersonal relatons, The survival is robust but not very challenging in itself, only obfuse in its mechanics. The tactics are a solid base but seldom become interesting. There is little room for creativity currently and it is mostly trading blows with opponents that you hopefully outnumber. The world is grittyish, but not really deep beyond standard medieavalist fare.The game looks certainly pretty and all the ingredients are there. There is simply not enough at the level of quality (currently) where I could have fun with it. The quite hefty price tag of 35 euros was enough for me to ask (and get) a refund. I'll certainly consider rebuying it when it has left Early Access and reviews are promising.

candidates.text: Its fun for a little bit until you realize you're in a loop of doing the same ♥♥♥♥ over and over again and nothing changes, the definition of insanity. You get more party members but now you're fighting more enemies and every fight is taking forever to the point it gets very old. The game also goes by Divinity difficulty settings which means on higher difficulty the enemies will have more health and do more damage to your mercs who are literally the same level and class. But lower difficulty is so easy that its boring af and none of your people are ever at risk because you just run through every enemy you face with ease. You can still get a lot of hours in this and have fun but eventually you will hit a wall and realize you have pretty much seen all of the game play this game has to offer in terms of features. It comes off as a deep squad management open world survival rpg but really its just a barebones one that has gives you zero sentimental value towards your company members, i played 20 hours and i didnt give af about any of my people and about 10-12 died in my play through, 3/4 of my starting members died pretty quickly into the game and i literally couldn't have cared less. The game just does a really bad job in providing a narrative or just some type of crisis that makes you care for these people, they try with the campfire talks but really that's the only time you can actually see any character or life inside of your members and it still doesn't matter because the ♥♥♥♥ they say isn't well written in the sense that "oh ♥♥♥♥ that was deep" or "i really like this guy". The members usually just say the stupidest ♥♥♥♥ that has nothing to do with anything and than the game gives you dialogue options that have little to zero effect on the party or character. I want to recommend Wartales but its just boring, period I regret buying it even though i had fun for a little bit.

candidates.title: Wartales review
candidates.text: This is ABSOLUTELY the sort of game you need to watch a no commentary gameplay video for. Within the first 15 minutes you're either going to love it or find it boring, and that stance is very unlikely to change even after playing dozens of hours. Wartales is fantastic, but it's very niche. If you've been craving a slow paced, grounded, party-based adventure in a low-fantasy world with a heavy focus on trade, inventory management, and exploration then this is your game. However, if any single part of that sounds tedious then the entire game falls apart. Like most games in this genre, there is combat and it's turn-based tactical. It's fun at first, but there's no auto-resolve feature to complete fights so fighting can become tedious on the hardest difficulty. To me, that reinforces the role playing aspect though - roving bands of outlaws should be avoided, not attacked just because it's free XP and loot. If you get tired of combat, you can always lower the difficulty on the fly to make fights a breeze. On the bright side, if you like the bones of the game but there are parts of it that annoy you there are mods available right now. Once you get the hang of it, modding the game yourself is quite simple. The devs are (allegedly) looking to allow Steam workshop support too, so modding could become even better in the future. That really makes a huge difference in a game like this, because there are a lot of things that just weren't quite right for me that the modding tool let me change.

candidates.text: 最重要的先说：这个游戏不是开放世界游戏，而是彻头彻尾的包含支线的线性RPG1.资源：有经营要素，但是大部分资源都是不可再生资源。跑商完全入不敷出，口粮与工资使得玩家被迫开图推剧情。2.地图与剧情：抛开弱智的导航不说，各个场景的内容是很贫瘠的。已经探索过的地图无法支撑玩家继续游玩，必须要根据主线流程推进到新地图。然而在新地图不过是用+12神圣璀璨史诗木棒殴打狂暴魔化传说野猪。3.人物：人物的成长有肉鸽要素，但是perk选择很少，随机出来的天赋也不具备显著的联动效应。总得来说，愿意玩的话可以游玩几十个小时，但是游戏的内容在10个小时以内基本可以体验完毕，剩下的时间就是重复劳动了。而且有资源紧张的紧迫感，对休闲玩家和种田玩家并不友好。

candidates.title: Wartales review
candidates.text: This is a very great game that i can highly recommend. If you enjoy mercenary/merchant company management (similar to mount and blade but smaller scale and more hardcore) than you will enjoy this game. I am still on my first game and there were moments where i almost lost everything. The game does a good job of making the start of the game feel like a grind. I constantly had the thought of "will things ever get better" run through my head as i was playing this. After hours a taking fights carefully, learning how to craft my own equipment and meals/medicine i was able to make it to where i can take most contracts without having high risk for low reward. It does suck how the beginning is a grind but in the end that just makes it all the more enjoyable and immersive. As you see your company grow from 4 farm boys with rags and sticks to professional mercenaries with iron plate armor and swords it makes you feel a sense of accomplishment. I did decide to play on region lock so that may be why i had such a hard time (makes different areas have higher or lowers level enemies. other mode has all enemies scale to you). Overall this is a great title that i did not expect to enjoy so much and think it is definitely worth the price tag. I would say some polish needs to be added (mostly with tool tips not going away or company path finding on the map) but a great game none of the less.

candidates.title: Subnautica: Below Zero review
candidates.text: This game expands upon the original Subnautica in every way possible: The graphics are significantly better, with far prettier biomes and effects. The STORY, well it has actual VOICE ACTING and real characters with personality, and you become so invested in the story as it goes on. There are better base parts with more customisation, and the crafting menus are easier to use, with features like the ability to pin recipies to your HUD. Overall, Below Zero expands upon my favourite aspects of the original game in the best ways, and it is a must-have for anyone who enjoyed the original.

candidates.title: Ability Scores (BG3)
candidates.text:
Ability Scores, or Abilities for short, are a game mechanic in Baldur's Gate III. They are basic physical and mental attributes that measure a creature’s capabilities. There are six abilities: Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma.

During Character Creation, Ability Scores are given default values based on the selected class. The player can then redistribute 27 of these points, raising or lowering abilities between a minimum of 8 and a maximum of 15. Raising an ability score by +1 costs 1 point, until it reaches 13 points; raising it above 13 costs 2 points for each +1 increase.

In addition, bonuses of +1 and +2 can be applied to two ability scores, potentially raising them as high as 16 or 17.

The character's Primary Ability is marked with a star, depending on the class's specialty. For spellcasters it's the ability uses for spellcasting; for other classes it's the ability used for melee or ranged attacks.

At Class levels 4, 8, and 12, a character can earn 2 additional points that can be applied to one ability or split between two abilities, to a maximum score of 20.

candidates.title: The Henry Stickmin Collection review
candidates.text: A fun remaster of all of the old games and a final sendoff for the series that is fantastic. That's really all that there is to say about this game. There is very little replay-ability, and there is very little that is new for those who have previously played the old Flash versions. The graphics are improved, but being able to choose between some of the older graphics and newer graphics for the previous games that are included would be a nice little addition. For a choose-your-own-adventure style game, $15 seems pretty high, especially for the amount of play time that you can get out of the game.Moral of the story: Fun if you've never seen anything related to it before, somewhat expensive for what you get (considering you can get a similar experience by watching videos about people playing this game), and ZERO replay-ability.It's a neat game and it's fun to look at, but other than that, it's like a book. Everything is scripted and will not change. Aside from what path is chosen, there is nothing you can really do anyways. Either way, I do appreciate this game being preserved on Steam. That is my favorite part of this game.

candidates.title: Wartales review
candidates.text: Pros: Wonderful replay-ability, a lot of different playstyles can be adapted, fun storyline with entertaining voice actors, good tactical gameplay, good overall strategy for a mercenary group... Basically it's a lot like a more graphically appealing version of say Battle Brothers, but instead of a procedurally generated map, it's the same map and quests with different adversaries and strengths.Cons: While it does have a lot of replay-ability, because the map and enemies are static, there's not too much going on in terms of "oh something new!", once you've seen it, you've seen it all, sort of things. There's kinda a lot of repetitiveness to the game play as well. Once you get to higher levels, it's just a matter of mitigating enemies and dealing as much damage as possible every turn.Overall: Worth it and fun. Needs some more improvements and additional content but definitely has great bones and wonderful potential. Go Devs!

candidates.title: IXION review
candidates.text: Re-edit after completing the game/ To start, the art, visuals, and story of this game are pretty good.The main problem I now have with this game is the replay value. Once you've beaten it I fail to see how there could be any more surprises. The story is very linear and there is only the one story, There are however a few different story elements based on choices you make which I think hardly constitutes a full replay. For the price I feel the length of the game is not worth it. I can see why they went with the price though again, it is visually very pretty and the story is good. The time spent isn't strictly always exploring. A lot of it is just sitting around watching a movie while you wait for research points, if you're like me at least. Some things that may bug you as a first time player. I had to restart this game half way through the third chapter because of a bug that was present at launch. They had patched the accident bug but, it didn't seem to be working. As soon as I started a new save, I never got one single accident the entire time from start to finish of the game. Even still, you will most likely end up restarting because there are a few frustrating things that can happen in terms of gameplay that will lead to a spiral of death. Restarting in this game felt terrible because of how long it takes to get back to where you were in the development of the ship.Last real complaint, you are punished harshly for not having meta knowledge of the game. That would be ok but again, restarting feels terrible. Teching back up takes a very long time, even with full upgrades to the tech lab. I would rate this game as a 3/5. I don't think it's purely terrible. It just feels like there could have been more to it than there was.

No excuses here. Cash grab move by 2K. I won't forgive that.- DRM and 5 activations of the game in a 24 limit. Yep. No clue why they bother with this... specially with the game opening limit- The story is not as great as borderlands 2... frankly it's just better than borderlands 1 story. candidates.title: Borderlands 3 review
candidates.text: In a way, i'm a little upset with myself for not enjoying B3 as much as everyone else says I should. I grew up playing Borderlands, and like so many others I've fallen in love with the series. The words "there's never been a bad Borderlands" game definitely have come out my mouth before.That is, however, up until Borderlands 3. Now I'll keep it real with you, its not . I've 100% played games 10x as worse than this. That doesn't mean this bad for an addition to the Borderlands series. In my mind, its comparable to how Fallout 4 was a bad Fallout, but a good game. You know what I mean?The pacing is off, the gameplay is not really evolved at all from prior entries, the voice-acting is sub-par (which is saying something for a Borderlands game), the characters feel gimmicky and barely thought-out, and somehow they managed to make a Borderlands game . How in the hell do you manage that?Anyways, what I think i'm trying to say is that although Borderlands 3 is not a horrific game on it's own, it is certainly the disappointment of the Borderlands family. My personal recommendation is to wait until its on sale, and then give it a try. Its certainly not worth the full $60.

candidates.title: Borderlands 3 review
candidates.text: I'm a casual player of Borderlands. I like the world, characters, art-direction, and over the top silly humor. I also like the world building as well. Borderlands 2 and TPS were pretty fun story-wise. However B3 story could've been done better. It had some really cool concepts, but the execution needed more work. I saw some behind the scenes director's cut ideas, but sad that they didn't make it to the actual game, as they could've really helped flesh out the story more. Overall, I still enjoyed Borderlands 3 though, despite my frustrations sometimes with the story and how they treated the characters. I also really loveeeed Bounty of Blood dlc. At first I didn't think I would. I thought it would just be another wasteland planet with boring people, but it really changed as I went along and I really loved the whole vibe and unique locations. The art direction, unique settings, and last but not least the characters you can play as were really amazing in B3. I played every character at once! I enjoyed each one and didn't get bored. This was a huge improvement compared to previous games. I also love that more legendary guns were accessible to casual players without excessive grind. Maybe too many, but still, I loved it. Allowed me to have fun as I'm mostly a solo player. I think for future Borderlands game, take the story at its own pace. Keep it fun and amazing with the silly humor, but during sad moments, let the game breathe and take it slow. A good balance of highs and lows really makes a whole lot of difference in story-telling. I really wish B3 had that in its main campaign. But still, overall, I love the game. Looking forward to B4 and hope it's better with a better story and a fun new cast of exciting characters.

The vault hunters were so unique and cool and fast traveling whenever was so nice. Once I played the other games after the 3rd one I realized the 3rd one is really only good because of how modernized it is compared to the others. But that's not a bad thing. Overall, I'd say this game is probably my favorite game of all time. Going to different planets was amazing and so unique to play. The loot was super cool too because of the guardian rank and being able to level up your luck with loot. Collecting was very fun in this game and I made lots of memories playing it. I've played through the story at least 13 times and wasn't disapointed during any of it. I recommend this game to people that have played the previous games first because it was confusing as hell seeing these characters I don't know. candidates.title: Embark on a journey in Cycles Reforged Update!
candidates.text:
Q: The Sealed Biome looks just like a regular biome. Is this intended?
This Update focuses solely on the Cycle overhaul (which is the foundation for any future work). We've been working on the build-up, not the climax (yet). On the journey before destination (sorry/not sorry for the blatant Brandon Sanderson reference).

The current Sealed Biome is just a placeholder and we're already in the middle of designing a proper new biome with unique visuals, music, and a potential mechanic for reforging the Seal. We expect to deliver it in late July or early August (this is, of course, subject to change).

You can see a sneak peek of the new biome above.

Q: Is there any content gated behind difficulty zones?
The World Map is divided into difficulty zones with each Seal marking the border of the particular difficulty. Playing farther away than the zone’s border will require you to play on a higher difficulty.
The aim here is to:

- Encourage players to amp up the difficulty as part of the game’s natural progression.
- Prevent situations when it would be optimal to play the last games in a Cycle (before attempting to close the Seal) on lower difficulties to accumulate negative modifier bonuses.

No actual content is gated behind the difficulty. You can still encounter each of the game’s Modifiers within the Settler difficulty zone.

We consider adding cosmetic rewards for completing Seals in the future. In our conversations with players, this was generally agreed on to be rewarding enough for those who complete them and not a deal-breaker for players who don’t aim to play on higher difficulties. We encourage you to share your thoughts with us too!

- Seal difficulty now works just like any other tile’s difficulty. The minimum difficulty is, like with any other field, determined by the distance from the Citadel.

- The difficulty level no longer influences the number of Embarkation Points.

- Embarkation Points are now related to the distance from the Smoldering City. The farther you play, the fewer Embarkation Points you have. Affects only the Base Pool, not the Reserve Pool.

- Changed how modifiers are spawned on the World Map. Positive modifiers are now more likely to appear around the Citadel, while negative ones will spawn further away (this isn’t a hard rule, negative modifiers might still spawn near the Smoldering City, just more rarely).

candidates.title: Introduction to Havoc Q&A - Dev Blog
candidates.text:
Answer
Havoc is not locked to a specific character, “ergo” Havoc is account-wide. With Havoc our intent is for players to adapt to the Havoc Assignment at hand by selecting the correct character, talents, weapons, blessing and curios to best take on the challenge. However, your character still needs to be level 30 to be able to join a Havoc mission.

Question
Will new garb be also character locked then? (Level up operative to gain access to new Moebian cosmetics for that class).

Answer
The cosmetics from Havoc are account-wide. (The same as any other cosmetic in the game.)

Question
What determines the max difficulty that I can currently play?

Answer
As long as a player is level 30 and can find a group that is willing to take them along, a player could in theory play any Assignment level at any time.

Question
Do I get access to a difficulty, based on my current highest completed? Can I access all difficulties <= my current max, or only 1 diff at a time?

Answer
At all times you have access to your own Assignment. If you feel like playing a lower Assignment level the way to do so would be to find a party with a lower Assignment level in the party finder and vice versa if you are looking for a higher Assignment level than what you currently own.

Question
Does my max available mission difficulty get reset every week?

Answer
Your maximum available mission difficulty will move forward with you into the next week. Each week players will get a new Havoc Assignment based on the highest Assignment they completed the previous week.

Question
Do i need to play from diff 1-40 within a single week in order to get to rank 40, unless i just join someone else's high diff mission?

Answer
No, you will continue the next week at the same level that you left off the previous week. The only thing that is weekly dependent is the weekly reward that is based on the highest-ranked mission you completed during the week.

candidates.title: Seal Contracts Update out now!
candidates.text:
But Seal Contracts aren’t the only big thing coming in this update. We also bring you 3 brand-new World Events. They are mostly centered around exchanging Citadel Resources (as a way of helping players in their Smoldering City progression) and spawning selected modifiers (as a way of combating some bad RNG when hunting for Deeds). Additionally, we also changed how the World Map is generated. From now on, after reforging the Gold Seal (Viceroy difficulty), there will be more modifiers and events in general and spawn rates will be shifted more in favor of negative modifiers rather than positive ones.

Fishmen Tribe

Balance-wise, this update brings a whole host of community-inspired tweaks. Most importantly, we decided to change the Prestige 15 difficulty modifier. Instead of prolonging the Storm, it now increases the threshold of Resolve required to generate Reputation after each earned point. However, this doesn’t mean the Storm will become shorter in Prestige games. We simply moved the Storm duration effect to the Viceroy difficulty, making it no longer a Prestige modifier, but a regular stat increase.

Now, why did we do this? Mainly because Storm duration effects are a double-edged sword. On one hand, they make the game harder, as players need to withstand hostile conditions for a longer period. On the other hand, at a certain point, a longer Storm is more of a bonus than a penalty (for example, by prolonging each year and making it easier to achieve certain objectives or postponing Hostility increases). That’s why we decided it would make for a good challenge on earlier difficulty levels, especially considering that a lot of recent updates have introduced various buffs and additional ways of dealing with setbacks, and there was always an effect missing between Veteran and Prestige 1 (both Veteran and Viceroy had the “Blight & Corruption” tag in the Embarkation Panel).

candidates.title: Embark on a journey in Cycles Reforged Update!
candidates.text:
- Ancient Seals can be found on the World Map. These intricate structures were built by a long-forgotten civilization, and it is believed that they hold a primeval, malevolent force at bay - the so-called Sealed Ones. Unfortunately, the power of the Seals has gradually waned over the millennia, causing the Sealed Ones to slowly regain their hold on this world. Your goal as the Queen’s Viceroy isn’t just to establish settlements and collect resources, but also to reforge these Ancient Seals and help the Crown protect the kingdom.
- To reforge a Seal, you will have to journey towards it with your caravan, collect enough Seal Fragments on the way there (a new Cycle-specific meta resource gained by winning games and completing modifiers), and successfully settle right next to it at the very end of the Cycle. If you make it there much sooner, you can wait until the end of the Cycle by pressing the button in the lower right corner of the screen.
- There are 8 types of Seals with distinct names and symbols. Each one requires more Seal Fragments and is located further away from the Smoldering City. At any given time, you can only see a maximum of four Seals on the World Map (two of the same type as the recently completed one, and two new ones). Successfully reforging a Seal will grant you additional Citadel Resources at the end of the Cycle and prolong the time between future Blightstorms by a few years.
- At the end of a Cycle leftover Seal Fragments must be returned to the Crown (for an additional reward).
- To attempt reforging a Seal, you have to:

- Have enough Seal Fragments.
- Be in range of the Seal.
- Be at the end of the Cycle (you can skip to it now by pressing the button on the calendar).
- Play at the minimum required difficulty level of the Seal (or higher).

After reforging a Seal and completing a Cycle, a new higher-tier Seal will spawn on the World Map (and the one that you just completed) as explained above.

You will also get additional Citadel Resources (a percentage value of all Citadel Resources that you collected during this Cycle).

In the Smoldering City, you will see the Highest Seal that you reforged.

Q: How does playing on the Sealed Biome differ for every Seal?
The Sealed Biome (Sealed Forest) will have exactly the same visuals, the same music, and the same mechanic on every difficulty level - there's no difference here no matter if you're playing on Settler or Prestige 20.

The difficulty may be scaled in some aspects aside from the regular increase in difficulty between levels.

Q: Do you unlock difficulty levels by reforging Seals?
No. The difficulty ladder and the Seal ladder are two different features. You unlock higher difficulties by winning games on the current highest difficulty. You can do this on every biome in the game and at any time during the Cycle. You can unlock Prestige 20 even if you never reforged any Seal.

Q: I still can’t make up my mind. What should I choose?
In our opinion, there’s no bad option here.

If you decide to start from the first - Bronze - Seal, you can always play it on a higher difficulty than the minimum one. However, you will start with the Base number of Years per Cycle (32 years). You can also skip to the end of the Cycle if you reach the Seal early.

However, if you don’t want to play multiple Cycles to get additional years that you’d normally get for reforging all the Seals up to the highest difficulty that you unlocked, you may choose the second option and start from a higher-level Seal. You will get all the additional years.

candidates.title: Hotfix 0.53.3 + additional information regarding the Seal progress transfer
candidates.text:
Q: What are the Seals?
The Ancient Seals are a new World Map system. Your task is to journey toward the Seal, gather enough Seal Fragments (necessary to play near the Seal) on the way, and when the Cycle is almost at its end, you can attempt to play on the Sealed Biome. By winning a game on the Sealed Biome, you successfully reforge a Seal.

Q: What dictates the Seal’s difficulty?
The Cycles Reforged Update introduced difficulty rings to the World Map. Due to the increasing distance from the Smoldering City’s line of supplies, it is more difficult for Viceroys to settle the farther they are from the Citadel.

Each Seal is located a bit farther from the other and each is located in a different difficulty ring.

Q: How many Seals are there?

- There 8 Seals you can complete in total:
- Bronze Seal (Settler and up)
- Lead Seal (Pioneer and up)
- Silver Seal (Veteran and up)
- Gold Seal (Viceroy and up)
- Platinum Seal (Prestige 5 and up)
- Cobalt Seal (Prestige 10 and up)
- Titanium Seal (Prestige 15 and up)
- Adamantine Seal (Prestige 20)

During each Cycle, 4 Seals will spawn on the World Map:

- 2 Seals of the highest difficulty that you already reforged
- 2 Seals of a higher difficulty than the highest one you reforged

For example: When you reforge a Silver Seal, during the next Cycle, 4 Seals will spawn: 2 Silver Seals and 2 Gold Seals. Lead Seals will no longer spawn on the World Map.

Q: What are the rewards for reforging a Seal?
By reforging each Seal, you get additional 8 years added permanently to the Cycle. It’s a one-time reward and you won’t get additional years for reforging the same Seal twice.

candidates.title: In Stars And Time review
candidates.text: A very excellently written little RPG with surprisingly human and resonant characters. I didn't quite know what to expect going in initially, but I was pretty quickly charmed by the cast. I was pretty consistently surprised by how many things in the game were reactive to my choices, and all of the little deviations really made for both some interesting sleuthing and some drove home some of the greater themes of the story.It's not without some flaws, chief of which I think is the friction that can come from replaying sections as a result of the looping mechanic. There are mechanics in the game that help ease the burden here, but depending on how you play you may stumble across some of them fairly early or quite late. For me some of the major ones came late in my play through, so I did feel some drag, but even so it wasn't enough to put me off. If this game looks appealing to you at all, I'd definitely suggest checking it out. I'm sure you'll be surprised.

candidates.text: Je viens tout juste de le finir et c'était très sympa. candidates.title: In Stars And Time review
candidates.text: In Stars and Time is, at its core, an RPG that effectively uses a time loop as a metaphor for depression. It's also a lot more than that. While not without some flaws, and aspects that will frustrate some players, I'm glad to have played it and would recommend it to anyone who doesn't mind repetition and backtracking, as long as they're used with purpose.My favorite thing about In Stars and Time is its characters and their dialogue. I genuinely enjoyed each and every one of them, and what they had to say to each other. It's rare that I like a main cast so well, or so quickly into a game (in fact, I fell in love with them back in my time with them in the demo, and at under a half hour into it).The story itself is also a highlight. As I started out by saying, the time loop in the story allowed the game to explore depression. There's the feeling of being trapped as attempts at trying new things lead to the same result with no escape at hand. Siffrin, the protagonist and only member of your party that remembers things from loop to loop, makes the decision to hide that they're looping through time. And this reminded me very much of how there have been times that I've tried to put on a convincing cheery facade at points I've been struggling. And that's just the tip of the iceberg!Besides exploring topics of mental health, the game explores LGBTQ+ themes in ways I appreciated. All of the party is queer in one way or another, and a couple of the characters have their identites explored in meaningful ways.

candidates.title: In Stars And Time review
candidates.text: All of the party is queer in one way or another, and a couple of the characters have their identites explored in meaningful ways. Beyond that, the culture of the country the game takes place in seems to center queerness, doing things like giving a child multiple names so that they can choose which one feels most comfortable when they become able to, for example, or how a branch of the world's magic system allows people to modify their bodies in gender-affirming ways.The worldbuilding is also fantastic. The game rewards you for checking every single item in every single room, often triggering conversations within the party. For example, that detail I just mentioned, about parents picking out multiple names for their children? That came from examining a stack of papers in a corner of a room! These conversations shed light on many different things including locations in the world, their cultures, the adventures that your party went on before it got trapped in a time loop, and more. I really enjoyed how one minor detail that I first came across in what felt like a throw-away conversation ended up being the first hint that I got towards a major plot point that was explored later on. The game rewards paying attention to this sort of thing.That, however, ties into the game's biggest flaw. It's sort of a necessary flaw for the story being told, but it's something that will turn some people away. A time loop that is fairly linear gets old pretty quickly. There's basically a single dungeon in the game, and you have to play through it many times. You do get the ability to fast forward conversations you've heard before, but this is a double-edged sword since it will sometimes also skip past new content. If something is truly important to the plot, the game will make sure you don't do that, but smaller details can be missed.The last thing I'll mention is the combat. The combat is based around a literal rock/paper/scissors system of weaknesses.

candidates.title: In Stars And Time review
candidates.text: A fun, unique game that explores the narrative themes of time loops and its psychological toll incredibly well. If you come into the game expecting a traditional RPG, this might not be the game for you. The RPG mechanics are simple, but fun enough to remain engaging for a time. I do appreciate that most of the equipment you get are more akin to side-grades than just higher numbers (Like lowering stats slightly to increase the potency of consumable items, or increasing attack at the cost of speed). It's a shame that, after the halfway point of the game, the RPG part no longer matters. Yes, you do still get new skills and items, but at that point you are so overpowered that they're only useful to clear encounters 5 seconds faster. If you only want to play this game for the gameplay, I can imagine one would find it tedious pretty fast.No, what makes this game truly special, is its narrative. Every character is lovingly written and drawn, with many animations/portraits brimming with personality. (according to a stream from jelloapocalypse, there are almost 500 portraits drawn for this game?!?) Your party chimes in with comments on the many, many, MANY objects you can interact with, often leading to long world building tangents about you, your party and the world. It can seem daunting, but I thoroughly enjoyed reading everything, oftentimes experimenting to see what kind of reactions the party would have based on your actions. It helps that there are several quality of life features present to cut potential tedium, such as fast-forwarding dialogue you have already seen, keeping all equipment between loops, a general hint system, and having multiple points of time you can warp too.

candidates.title: In Stars And Time review
candidates.text: I finished the game after 16 hours, and can give my impressions. I don't know if there are multiple endings, and I definitely found most things but didn't find everything (all accessories/weapons but not all memories). This is a great game if you like emotional stories, light RPG mechanics, the art style, and are queer or an ally. The game uses its timeloop format intertwined with the story and characters in a smart way to approach difficult themes and guide the characters through them. It is similar to Undertale, but while the game is goofy when it wants to be and not every joke will land with you, it is not nearly as "internet-humor", "lol so random" as parts of Undertale are. Characters in this are far, far more relatable and their issues are grounded, approached, solved in an intelligent and mature way. Or not ultimately solved! Some things don't get fixed right away and that's ok, in fact a refreshing take on how real life works. In my opinion the game is written very well, overall. You will see aspects of yourself and the people you know in these characters, hell you may BE one of these characters. As you can see in one of the main tags of the game, the game does feature a lot of LGTBQ+ characters and themes, and like I mentioned above, it handles this in a very respectful, intelligent, mature way. Being LGTBQ+ is not what the game is all about, the game instead tells the story centering around the main character of Siffrin, and just happens to star characters that mirror the LGTBQ+ community and aspects of our own lives. I mean this game takes place in a country that worships change as a religion, and changing your entire physical makeup is magically as easy as the equivalent of going to get a fancy haircut. So in a setting like this, the question you explore is what are the issues that the characters face? Are they similar/different?

candidates.title: In Stars And Time review
candidates.text: As a piece of art, In Stars and Time has a lot to say and excels at putting you in the headspace of the playable character, Siffrin, even before you reach the ending. As a game, it is a frustrating mess of oldschool adventure game-esque "gotcha" moments that force you to trudge back through dialogue (only some of which is skippable) and forced combat to return to your spot.I absolutely loved the cast of this game. The characters have such charm and there is a great deal of love and care put into writing their interactions as both natural and informative to the player (particularly about worldbuilding). In Stars And Time presents its cast and themes in such an exquisite way that I found myself wanting to push forward just to glean the next kernel of information.However, the moment-to-moment gameplay was repetitive at best and infuriating at worst. The game makes full use of its narrative theme of loops to the detriment of the play experience, overusing moments of forced backtracking through tens of minutes of content.As an example, I would espy a suspicious object, be unable to interact with it in a meaningful way, and then being later told that of it's suspicious and that I should have searched more thoroughly was exhausting. Siffrin internalizes this frustration whereas I feel like I have had my time wasted. candidates.title: In Stars And Time review
candidates.text: WARNING: If "woke" games make you cringe, skip this one.For everyone else who doesn't think having gay or trans people in a videogame is some kind of sin against God, In Stars and Time is a charming indie title that uses RPG tropes and mechanics, and player-driven curiosity to tell a complex and extremely compelling character driven story. RPG battles, levels and equipment are less about challenging the player strategically (tho that aspect does exist a little bit) and more used as tools to subtly enhance the themes of the story by tying them to mechanics.This is a full-length 40 hour game made by a tiny studio, and while it is intentionally repetitive you will always feel like you're moving forward and making progress. You'll want to check the same items, objects, and locations, talk to the same people over and over to see what changes with each new time loop - and a lot of the time that curiosity will be rewarded. Music is retro inspired, catchy, and has a lot of nuanced variations to fit different emotional tones and situations. The artwork is abundant and stylish, if simple. It conveys a lot of emotion, which I think is key for a game like this. But most of all, the writing is exceptional. This game will probably make you cry. 10 Gallons of Tears out of 10.

You know what you have to do.From the top, again.Ultimately, the game excels at its character interactions, with heartfelt and sincere moments of bonding. More than its psychological horror coating, more than its overarching lore puzzle, the game explores themes of found family, agency, consent and forgiveness, with moving (if a little didactic) ace/aro, trans, masc gay romance representation, and more. The pacing gets frantic, with back-loaded twists, culminating in emotional catharsis that may feel like it's going a bit everywhere at once - though still managing to land on its feet. After finishing the game, you're left with the sense you've experienced something precious, an individual voice echoing through the craft, a vision that shines through and overpowers the systemic warts, the questionable pacing, the dreary repetition. candidates.title: Bitburner review
candidates.text: Bitburner is a game that feels like it was tailor-made for those who ever thought, "What if writing cheats for Counter-Strike 2 was its own game?" In this idle-style simulation, you're thrust into a cyberpunk world where your primary weapon isn't a gun but JavaScript. Unlike traditional idle games where you simply click away mindlessly, Bitburner demands that you engage your brain cells to write scripts that automate the very grind you're trying to bypass. It's essentially what would happen if you took the scripting grind of cheating in CS2 and turned it into a game—a surprisingly addictive one at that.The premise is deceptively simple: hack your way through a dystopian future by writing increasingly complex scripts. The game slowly pulls you in with straightforward tasks but quickly escalates into a brain-teaser that has you optimizing your code to squeeze every last bit of efficiency out of your virtual heists. It's like you've stepped into a cybercriminal's shoes, only instead of shady backroom deals, you're fine-tuning algorithms.What makes Bitburner so engaging is its educational twist. As you progress, you'll find yourself learning actual JavaScript, making it more than just a game—it's a coding boot camp wrapped in a neon-drenched shell. For those with a programming background, it's a playground to flex your coding muscles, while beginners might find themselves gaining useful skills without even realizing it. However, it’s not without its challenges; the learning curve can feel like diving into the deep end of a pool, especially for those unfamiliar with programming.Visually, Bitburner keeps things minimalist, which fits its hacker aesthetic perfectly. The UI is essentially a fancy terminal, which might not be everyone’s cup of tea but works wonders for immersion.

candidates.title: Grand Tactician: The Civil War (1861-1865) review
candidates.text: 難易度very easyではありますが、1861年シナリオの南軍で勝利することができたので、自分が分かる限りのことをレビューさせていただきます。 まず、このゲームは知名度があまりありません。 日本においては皆無といって良いと思います。 当然日本語化MODもなければ日本語の情報もほとんどないです。 それでも、内容としてはこれ以上にないと思います。 南北戦争を描いたゲーム自体少ないかと思いますが、このゲームは細かいところまで精密に描写しています。 まず戦闘面においては、"ORDER DELAY"というシステムが搭載されています。 （設定でオフにすることもできます）軍隊は指揮官を通して命令を実行するわけですが、この時代には当然、電信はあっても無線機を兵士たちが所持している……なんてことはありません。 例えば軍団長が師団長に命令を発したとしたら、配下の人たちが馬に乗って師団長に命令を伝えに行きますし、師団長が各旅団長に命令を伝えるのにも、どうしても遅延が発生してしまいます。 部隊が遠くにいればその分命令を伝えるのに時間がかかってしまうので、できるだけ近くにいたほうがいい……といった感じです。 具体的には、"BUGLE RANGE"と"COMMAND RANGE"の二つがあります。 HQを中心に円状になっていて、BUGLE RANGEのなかにいればより早く命令が伝わりますし、より大きいサークルのCOMMAND RANGEのなかに居れば指揮官のボーナスが付与されます。 HQの位置が遠くて部隊に危機が迫っても中央司令部がすぐに対処することができない場合があったりすると、「自主的に対処してくれ……！ 」なんて思うことが多々あります。 個々の指揮官の自主性って大事なんだなあ。 別動隊を組織する場合は"AI STANCE"というのがあるので、これを設定しておくといい感じ。 例外ですが、自分のユニットを選択して敵ユニットを右クリックすると遅延なく攻撃することができます。 ビューグルとかドラム、手旗信号とかで攻撃命令を伝えてるのかな……。

candidates.title: Wingspan review
candidates.text: Wingspan is one of my favorite board games, if not my all-time favorite game. I don't think it's nearly as good as a digital experience and can't recommend it. This is an engine building game with very little interaction between players, and the loss of humans sitting at a table is too significant. The interface makes it difficult to keep track of what other players are even doing on their turns, so you're sort of left with your own board and no sense of how other players are doing on theirs, or even what birds they're playing. At my table, we always oooh and ahhhh over the birds as they are played and sometimes read the little trivia snippets to each other. In digital Wingspan it's hard to even know *when* another player is playing a bird since the interface does not naturally follow along with the actions of other players.Whether or not you're going to win feels like a crapshoot - and that's sort of how it is with tabletop Wingspan, but it's felt more keenly here since you won't be looking at the other boards very much, and you don't have anyone to talk to while you play.The automa mode is similarly diminished since, again, it's hard to follow along with how the automa is doing on its turns, so you're really just hoping you're doing better.Pretty disappointing! I'm not sure how this can be fixed. It just doesn't feel like a good fit for this medium.

candidates.title: IXION review
candidates.text: It's a wonderful space-station management game where you are tasked with acting as Administrator of the Tiqqun (the space-station) and all that it entails. I loved the premise of the game, the min-maxing of tiles/sectors, discovering more bits of the story with each chapter and trying to find a balance between risk and reward regarding space exploration. It's fun trying to decide how to handle the challanges of the game as you try to find a base-layout that will satisfy the needs of the station and it's inhabitants. Gripes with the game are the ones generally stated: morale-related spirals of doom that favours a "slow and steady"-approach over other playstyles, difficulities handling inter-sector trade and the occational need to save-scum to make plans to handle an event that lies ahead. All in all, it's a positive experience. Bonus points for a fitting soundtrack and eeire storylines.

Things like that, plus a very slow gameplay and complicated button operations sometimes make the game a test of patience. candidates.title: Valheim review
candidates.text: --An underwhelming experience for the survival game player.--Although i have only played 8 hours of game-play i have covered all of the essential game mechanics and to my surprise this a let down. Your initial goal in the first hours of playing is gathering, building a base and upgrading your tools and weapons, then you fight a boss. Once you beat a boss you get an ability then you move on to the next one. Your initial goal now is to gather, build a new base, upgrade your tools and fight the next boss. If you can see the pattern what I am saying is that Valheim is a repetitive mess. And the graphics don't help! --Overall Gameplay--You can try to make it enjoyable by moving around more, living in dangerous environments and doing creative challenges but the point is that the amount of content limits what you as the player can do. However, the main goal is to just get stacked build a base and defeat bosses. This can be a 'grindy' process for the casual player not to mention that this gets old fast when you realise that the environment is not lively at all and that there are no NPC's to meet (Other than the shop). This just makes the player feel like there is nothing else but their group of friends and that they won't come across something new. The abandoned villages are the only large structure on land and yet they are still extremely disappointing. They contain a couple chests beds and that's it. No story, no NPC's or some unique trait. The bosses are a great challenge and offer some really great opportunities to strategise but they are all still really easy to beat. --PvP--The first boss you encounter can be killed with just the first bow and a couple arrows and that's a BIG hint on what you are going to be coming across.

candidates.title: Valheim review
candidates.text: The game has its moments, like first taking off on a boat, appreciating your settlement after it's gotten to a certain size, fighting a troll for the first time... These things make the game enjoyable. Unfortunately, they are few and far between. What's occupying the rest of the time? Grinding resources--boar hides, copper, iron, etc. Once you start needing metal for all of your weapons, armor, tools, and upgrades, the game becomes a serious drag. You do almost nothing but search for new mining outcrops, crypts, etc. Even with a wagon, the process is unbearably slow and unfulfilling.The area you get iron from even seems designed to make people stop playing the game. I can understand making something challenging, but the challenges in this area are poisonous enemies, shuffling slowly through water as said enemies attack you, waiting for stamina to regenerate to raise more land, waiting for the right monster to spawn, creating new worlds specifically to farm more of these areas because they don't have enough buildings.The developers have included some cool features like deformable terrain, building structural integrity, and volumetric smoke/fog. The fighting is serviceable, but don't expect many surprises. I died to trees far more than I did to the bosses (never). When a group of small enemies provide more challenge and entertainment than a boss fight, it's not a good sign.If you have the masochism necessary to endure the grind, you will probably find many enjoyable moments in this game building cool settlements, fighting new monsters, and exploring new biomes. If you value your time, dislike spending the majority of your time mining, or appreciate a well thought-out world map, story, and occasionally having a conversation with an NPC, this game isn't for you.

candidates.title: Valheim review
candidates.text: I haven't felt this way about a video game since 2012 when my brother introduced me to a simple yet endlessly fun beta test game called Minecraft. Valheim is an incredible experience and everyone with an interest in survival, crafting, parry combat, vikings, or just casual fun gameplay should check it out. Graphics: ★★★★★-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Despite its low poly world design, Valheim does not look like a PS2 game. Somehow, through blooming and shadow detail and depth of field and a ton of other graphical enhancements, Valheim's relatively low-detail models look beautiful enough to make me forget that I'm even playing a video game. Gameplay: ★★★★★-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------I compare the gameplay to minecraft because my first night in Valheim felt so reminiscent of my first night in Minecraft, gathering basic materials, crafting primitive tools, and taking shelter in a hastily built home as night approached. I quickly discovered that combat in Valheim includes a rewarding block and parry system, as well as a dark souls style i-frame dodge mechanic. Blocking an enemy's projectile at the perfect moment will stun them, and offer enough time to roll forward and uppercut them with a fist, stab with a sword, or bash with a club. The combat system doesn't require high skill, but greatly rewards it. Story: ★★★★★-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Valheim's story acts as more of a framing device than a traditional narrative, and there are no cutscenes, dialogue, or voice acting. That being said, the game is best enjoyed cooperatively with multiple friends on the same world, and I loved making our own lore and story for the game. Valheim's world has a boss fight for each biome that will reward an item needed for the next biome to continue progression, and this progression loop is so satisfying.

candidates.title: Valheim review
candidates.text: I've played Valheim for over 3000 hours, and I can confidently say it is the best $20 I've ever spent! This game masterfully combines exploration and building, creating an experience that is both immersive and endlessly enjoyable.One of the standout features of Valheim is the balance it strikes between exploration and building. The biomes and scenery, while not boasting cutting-edge graphics, are beautifully crafted and create a captivating environment. Each biome feels distinct and offers unique challenges and resources, contributing to a sense of discovery and adventure.The game's development can sometimes feel slow, but the end results are always polished and satisfying. Each update brings new content and improvements that enhance the overall experience, demonstrating the developers' commitment to quality.Progression in Valheim is fun and challenging. It allows players to advance at their own pace without feeling pressured to rush. Whether you prefer tackling the game's challenges head-on or taking your time to build and explore, Valheim accommodates both playstyles beautifully.I've enjoyed the game both solo and with friends, playing with up to 8 players at once. The cooperative aspect is fantastic, and we've built some truly impressive structures together. From giant castles and sprawling towns to the great walls of the Plains and island fortresses, the building possibilities are virtually endless. There is so much to do if you have a builder's mindset, and the game provides ample tools and materials to let your creativity run wild.If I had to point out any weaknesses, it would be the lack of variation in the biomes. While each biome is beautifully crafted, more diversity would make exploration even more interesting and rewarding.

candidates.title: Path Of Wuxia review
candidates.text: It isn't a bad game, first off the graphics are not going to blow your mind. The art style however is very much left me satisfied. This is a SRPG with turn based combat and none of the complexity more modern SRPGs use to make things more active. With that said the games focus oddly doesn't seem to be the combat but rather the story being told and interactions with other students, and in that way the game is less so an SRPG and more so a Novel. This is an example of a still young genre that I think is inaccurately categorized as Martial Arts, this should instead be the Genre "Wuxia" in as much as we use "Fantasy" in the West and know what that's about. So on the game itself; If you are looking for a story about school life but with some wuxia elements thrown in - this is the game for you. I have to say that it is honestly close to me saying it's a kind of dating simulation but again Romance is part of Wuxia. There is a Discord community for the English translation which does a cracking job at it, but because of this I can't exactly say if the game does a good job of getting you interested in the drama of these npcs but the content here is certainly not lacking. There is an unfortunate grind to the game and a time table it forces on to you, there are no classic wuxia hidden benefits found in places that allow the MC a unique body tempering technique or heavenly scrolls of the gods gate qi manipulations. Instead you grind it out seemingly like everyone else. But you are special because you can change your element mid fight. This is pretty cool but a signal of the games only failure - the lack of content about the player themself. In Wuxia stories what engages people isn't the love interest or the friends but rather the Main Character and so far there is a problem here.Music is great, controls are good, it support controller as well though barely.

If you have problems trying to compile, or you find a specific error, please contact me at service@exlb.net or at github issue. I'll try to fix it.

Download and install Visual Studio 2022 Community

VisualStudio is the most comprehensive IDE developed by Microsoft for .NET and C# developers on Windows.

Just open it after downloading and install it, remembering to check Net Desktop Development and Universal Windows Platform Development

After that, go all the way to the next step and the installation is complete.
If you can't install it, it's a system problem, the program is a code editor developed by Microsoft.

2. Download VPet source code

Source: github https://github.com/LorisYounger/VPet/
Select download zip, then unzip

Once extracted, double-click on `VPet.sln` to open the VPet source code.

3. Start compiling

In the upper left corner of VisualStudio select X64 and VPet.Simulator.Windows

Click the dark green Run button to run VPet source code.

If everything runs fine, the game will report an error "缺少模组Core,无法启动桌宠\nMissing module Core, can't start up", as shown below

Next, open the `VPet-Simulator.Windows` folder in the folder where the code is located.
Right click to run mklink.bat as administrator

Next, re-click the dark green Run button to run the VPet source code, and it will run VPet normally!

candidates.title: HUMANKIND™ review
candidates.text: This is an okay game and it's nice to look at. There's some ideas in it that I like. But overall, there's a lot of things it doesn't quite stick the landing on -- and many of those things are things that Civilization VI DOES do well. Often, the logic behind design choices is difficult to follow.Some examples:- though the UI is stylized and nice, it often can be hard to read- minor AI civs are harder to understand and interact with, with too many numbers to track- few ways to use the game's built-in info to clarify what things are (a la Civilopedia)- combat is bizarre and counterintuitive, using a system that feels like it was a half-implemented good idea that falls flat and defies logic- Overall, it's smaller issues like this that take too much away from what could be a fun approach to city/civilization-building games. it's a beautiful game that just can't quite measure up to the giants of the genre.

candidates.title: Trials of Mana review
candidates.text: Trials of Mana is a cute and fun action RPG where you'll encounter puppies, bunnies, and pikachus... and beat the crap out of them for no good reason. Despite the childish visuals and story, the game has a deep class system that allows for plenty of creativity and customization. The game has some flaws, most of which don't apply if you just approach the game casually, but are quite annoying if you want to get more hardcore into the game.8/10Pros- The class system is really good. Each character has 4 different class paths they can take. With 6 total characters, this results in a lot of combinations and variety. There's a lot of replay value.- Combat, while simple, is fun and deeper than it initially seems. There's a lot of things to learn and a lot of things to be mindful of during combat.- Once you reach class 3, the game becomes incredibly fun. You get a lot of abilities that really open up what you can do in combat. After over 100 hours, I'm still having a blast trying out different combinations.- Graphics are cute and very good.- Angela is very sexy!Cons- AI is bad. They constantly get killed in boss fights (even in normal difficulty). They often just stand there instead of attacking enemies. They often sit on full resources without using abilities. They use random and useless abilities (player has zero control over which abilities they use). They don't do boss mechanics. They're slow to heal. While the game is easy enough that you can get through the game easily in hard difficulty and below, it's still hard to overlook such bad AI. AI needs to be better and the player really needs more settings to control AI behavior, such as enabling/disabling specific abilities.- Class 3 is where things really start to get fun with builds.

candidates.title: Dev Log: Combat System
candidates.text:
Hi engineers!

In the months following Dyson Sphere Program: Rise of the Dark Fog's showcase at TGS 2022, we received a lot of encouragement and support from our players. This has greatly motivated our team to put more effort into developing combat-related content. Let’s have a glance at the visuals we are currently working on:

During the combat system development, some optimization of existing gameplay systems was also introduced. Such as a new distribution logistics system, more advanced Chemical Plants, Splitters with storage, more convenient conveyor belt tools …

In order to maximize the team production effectiveness, we split our workflow into two branches - The Rise of the Dark Fog (combat system) branch and existing content updates. So that we can do these two parts of work at the same time, and keep the combat system info confidential. But we need to make sure to merge the changes made in the Update Branch into the Combat Branch from time to time, to ensure that the work on both sides is always in sync.

However, we also have a piece of bad news here: During the year that the combat system branch has been running separately, its content conflicts with the main branch have caused many code and resource issues. We had to put huge amounts of extra effort and time to resolve these problems every time, and sometimes we even have to deliberately avoid modifying common resources and low-level codes, which distracts us a lot from the combat system development. To speed up the progress of combat system development, we have decided to devote our full effort to the combat branch. In other words, we will still be able to debug and modify the existing game contents, but not be able to add any new features before the combat mode is grounding.

candidates.title: Temtem review
candidates.text: This game is amazing, it takes pokemon's already amazing combat systems and makes it even better with the new stamina system + the removal of RNG. Animations are amazing, music is great, visuals are stunning at times. Just a solid all round must play for fans of the genre.

candidates.title: Wartales review
candidates.text: Here we have the problem of:Battles:Battles start with deployment and an initiative chain on the bottom left - the initiative is well structured - I like it. The problem is that the battle map AND the deployment system soon mean that anyone who has come from a wargaming or a D&D environment is soon confronted with the absence of things we all recognise... like common sense.Characters are in different classes - tanks, wackers, squishies with knives or bows (the latter suck in melee - can't have a secondary weapon). Okay - one would assume that you could assume a formation or place your tanks out in front to draw the enemy's attention.That's when you run into the really really really stupid bit. You start deployed all over the map - I mean ALL OVER IT. The enemy are already mixed in with you, so the game expects the player to then work out, based on initiative order and the relative enemy types in that order, where to place his adventurers in order to lock up the dangerous enemies first.Only - you're scattered.Okay, you can redeploy into available blue deployment squares - but these are not all the movement spaces on the map and are oddly placed and limited. Which means in practice that against a same-level or level+1 enemy and one which likely outnumbers your group, that your squishy DPS types are going to get hit and your tanks are not going to be able to take on the enemy's tanks before your DPS types are on death's door.Also, I kind of expect that if my party attacks from the north that I would start grouped together...on the north side of the map. Apparently that's too easy and not skilful enough.Now we have the combat system.Bits of this make sense.
